rationale: Start with a broad, moderately fast gradient to locate all eight compounds and identify critical pairs near the 10-minute scoring window. The strong final solvent reduces the risk of missing highly retained compounds.

Keep the gradient fixed and raise temperature to test selectivity changes in the four-peak cluster and late doublet. All peaks currently elute well before 10 minutes, leaving room to slow the gradient later if needed.

Use a substantially shallower gradient at the better-performing temperature to spread the central cluster and probe slope-dependent selectivity. The current early elution window provides substantial room before the time penalty begins.
The shallower gradient resolves the central cluster, leaving just one critical pair. Lower temperature by one step to shift that pair's selectivity while retaining the improved gradient separation.

Lower the starting organic fraction to test whether stronger initial retention improves the remaining central doublet. Keep temperature and gradient duration near the best method, with some time margin below 10 minutes.

At 60 C the central cluster was fully resolved, so test a shallower gradient to move the remaining near-coeluting pair apart. Four additional gradient minutes should place the last peak close to the 10-minute target.
A shallower gradient at 60 C may finish separating the remaining doublet. Raise the starting organic fraction to offset the longer gradient and aim to keep the final peak within 10 minutes.

Test an intermediate slope on the faster side of the late-pair crossover seen at 60 C. A lower starting organic fraction should help preserve central-cluster separation while keeping the last peak comfortably below 10 minutes.

Make a small slope reduction from the nearly optimal injection 8 to lift the central doublet above R = 1.5. Monitor the later doublet closely, since its resolution may decrease as the gradient becomes shallower.

The two critical pairs trade resolution at 60 C, with no obvious intermediate slope on the grid at this starting composition. Test the low-temperature extreme for a different selectivity pattern while retaining the nearly optimal gradient as a reference.

Test the shallower-gradient side of the late-pair crossover, where resolution was improving in injection 6. A moderately higher starting organic fraction should limit the last retention time without sacrificing as much central-cluster resolution as injection 7.
Use a substantially shallower slope to move beyond the late-pair crossover and improve central-cluster separation. Raising the start to 0.20 should help keep the last peak near or below 10 minutes.

Refine around injection 8 with a higher starting organic fraction and a slightly shallower slope. This tests whether the central doublet can reach R = 1.5 while retaining enough separation in the later cluster.
Reduce the slope one step from injection 13 to improve both central doublets. The later critical pair has R = 1.78, which may provide just enough margin for all pairs to reach 1.5.

Use a slope of 0.045 organic fraction per minute, slightly steeper than injection 14, to lift the late doublet above 1.5 while preserving the central separations. The gradient should still extend beyond the last peak, so the lower endpoint should not affect elution.
Injection 15 reaches the maximum CRF. Test a slightly steeper gradient to shorten actual elution time while checking whether the narrow resolution margins remain above 1.5.

Keep injection 15 as the maximum-score benchmark and test a higher starting organic fraction for faster elution. Compensate with a shallower slope to recover central-cluster resolution rather than further steepening the gradient.
Test a slope between the fully resolved injection 15 and the slightly too-steep injection 16. This may shorten the last retention time while keeping every pair just above R = 1.5.

Injection 15 remains the fully resolved, maximum-score benchmark; steeper gradients at 60 C lose central resolution. Test a cooler selectivity regime near injection 10, using a higher starting organic fraction to reduce retention time.

Test whether lower-temperature selectivity resolves the central cluster with a faster gradient than injection 19. Injection 15 remains the maximum-score benchmark; this explores an alternative fully resolved method.
Test a steeper gradient at 30 C to shift the central cluster away from the near-coelution seen in injection 19 and shorten elution. Retain injection 15 as the established maximum-score method.

Test a shorter gradient followed by a hold, allowing the hold to alter the late-cluster separation rather than relying solely on gradient slope. Injection 15 remains the fully resolved maximum-score benchmark.

Keep the optimal gradient and test a lower-temperature selectivity regime for greater resolution margins. Injection 15 already achieves the maximum CRF and remains the benchmark unless this alternative is fully resolved and faster.

Return to 60 C and test a shorter programmed gradient with a slope just shallower than injection 15. This checks whether a lower solvent endpoint can retain full resolution; injection 15 remains the maximum-score benchmark.

Use the final injection to test temperature sensitivity one grid step below the optimal method while holding its gradient fixed. Injection 15 remains the established maximum-score method, with all pairs resolved and the last peak at 7.45 minutes.
